explanation:
## The program

```cpp
while (std::cin >> word)
{
    ++count;
    if (word.size() > longest.size()) longest = word;
}
```

## >> splits on whitespace, for free

Reading a `std::string` with `>>` does three things: skip any
leading whitespace, read characters until the next whitespace, and
leave that whitespace in the stream for next time. So a stream of
text becomes a stream of words with no splitting code at all, and
runs of spaces, tabs and newlines are all the same separator.

What it cannot do is tell you where the lines were, or treat
punctuation as a separator. `hello,` is one word here, which the
constraints say on purpose — a real word-counter would have to
define what a word is rather than inheriting the stream’s answer.

## The empty string as a starting value

The running-maximum problem again, and this time there *is* an
identity: the empty string has length 0, and every word read by `>>`
has length at least 1, so the first word always wins. No "is this
the first one" test is needed.

That is the difference from the integer version, where no `int` is
smaller than every other `int`. Worth noticing, because it explains
why one of the two problems needs a flag and the other does not.

## > keeps the first, >= keeps the last

```
cat dog

with >     cat beats "" ; dog does not beat cat   → cat
with >=    cat beats "" ; dog ties and replaces   → dog
```

Neither is wrong in general; only one answers the question as
asked. Whenever a problem says "the first" or "the last" of equals,
that sentence is telling you which comparison to write.

## size() is unsigned, and here it does not matter

`word.size()` is a `std::size_t`, and it is compared against another
`std::size_t`, so no conversion happens and no warning appears. It
is printed directly rather than stored in an `int`, for the same
reason. The moment you mix it with a signed `int` — `for (int i = 0;
i < word.size(); ++i)` — the comparison converts the `int` to
unsigned and `-Wsign-compare` has something to say.

## What this does not check

What counts as a word. Hyphens, apostrophes, numbers and
punctuation are all just characters to `>>`, so `well-known` is one
word and `end.` is five letters and a full stop. Defining a word
properly means deciding about all of those, which is a different
and much larger exercise.
